title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 22: The HRET at Work

primary_topics: Chapter 22 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's promised report on the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal, written on the first anniversary of his chairmanship, surveying the Tribunal's composition, its procedures, and every case it handled in the term following the May 10, 2004 elections.

A primer on HRET practice: the constitutional grant under Section 17 of Article VI making the Tribunal the sole judge of contests over the election, returns and qualifications of representatives, and the mechanics of protests and quo warranto petitions from summary dismissal under Rule 21 through summons, preliminary conference, revision and appreciation of ballots.

The Tribunal's docket and output under his watch: 15 election protests, 3 quo warranto petitions and 1 petition to re-canvass returns, of which 8 protests and all 3 quo warranto cases -- more than half the total -- had been disposed of by press time, with the dispositions recounted case by case.

The two substantive rulings given at length -- the quo warranto cases of San Miguel v. Dy on residence and animus revertendi and Samson v. Crisologo on the effect of an absolute pardon, and the protest of Roman v. Garcia, where revision and appreciation of ballots in all 881 precincts widened the protestee's margin from 803 to 1,417 votes.

Angping v. Roces, the case CJP calls the most controversial in terms of novelty of issue: a petition asking only for a re-canvassing of election returns, in which the Tribunal upheld the substitute candidacy and its own jurisdiction, and CJP wrote separately that the primordial duty of the Tribunal was to ascertain the true winner in the election.
sub_topics: The chapter's premise: having written in 'Leveling the Playing Field' that he enjoyed his role as HRET chairperson and saluted his brethren-lawmakers, CJP now redeems his commitment to report more extensively on the Tribunal.

The HRET's composition under Section 17, Article VI -- nine members, three justices designated by the Chief Justice with the senior justice as chairperson and six representatives chosen by proportional representation -- and the roster as of press time on October 10, 2005.

The distinction between an election protest, filed by a defeated candidate within ten days of proclamation on grounds of fraud or irregularities, and a quo warranto petition, filed by any voter of the district on the ground of disloyalty or ineligibility.
The novelty of a challenge to 'returns': the HRET Rules have no express provision for it and the contest type had not been tested before his term, until Angping v. Roces.

The five grounds for summary dismissal under Rule 21: insufficiency in form and substance, late filing under Rules 16 and 17, non-payment of the filing fee, non-payment of the cash deposit or its first P150,000, and illegibility of the petition and annexes.

The procedural sequence after summons under Rule 22: answer and counter-protest within ten days, joinder of issues under Rule 54, preliminary conference for simplification of issues, stipulations, limits on witnesses, evidence aliunde, withdrawal of precincts and dates for evidence, then a preliminary conference resolution.

The divergent tracks thereafter: a hearing commissioner receives evidence in quo warranto cases within twenty-day periods, while an election protest proceeds to collection of ballot boxes, revision under Rule 88 in pilot or all contested precincts, reception of evidence, and the Tribunal's appreciation of ballots.

The docket at the start of the term and the eight protests plus three quo warranto petitions disposed of -- Roco v. Villafuerte (withdrawal, with the counter-protestant denied his damages claim), San Juan v. Cerilles (insufficient in form and substance and lack of jurisdiction for failing to allege the proclamation), and Cerbo Jr. v. Mangudadatu (failure to file a reply).

Further dismissals: Calizo v. Miraflores (loss of interest and non-payment of the cash deposit), Kho v. Seachon, Hussin v. Amin (failure to state the precincts protested after a show-cause resolution), Liwag v. Cruz (failure to submit written arguments), and Andueza v. Bravo (filed beyond the period under Rule 16).

San Miguel v. Dy: a challenge to Rep. Consuelo A. Dy's residence in Pasay City, where the address in her Certificate of Candidacy was alleged to be a cockpit arena; witnesses, school certifications and her political career as councilor and representative persuaded the Tribunal of her domicile of origin and animus revertendi.

The doctrine applied there, citing Romualdez-Marcos v. Comelec: residence in election law is synonymous with domicile, an individual does not lose domicile by living and maintaining residences elsewhere, and a change requires actual and deliberate abandonment, with the burden on the petitioner.

Samson v. Crisologo: Rep. Vincent Crisologo, convicted of arson and arson with homicide in 1972, conditionally pardoned in 1981 and granted an absolute and unconditional pardon in 1986 restoring full civil and political rights, was challenged under Article 36 of the Revised Penal Code.

The Tribunal's two holdings in Crisologo: res judicata could not bar the case because jurisdiction shifts from the Comelec before proclamation to the HRET after it, and absolute pardon restoring full political rights removed all disabilities, including the rights to vote, to be voted for and to hold public office.

Roman v. Garcia: a protest over the 2nd District of Bataan, where Garcia led by 803 votes, 479 precincts were protested and 881 counter-protested, and the Tribunal dispensed with pilot precincts and ordered revision and appreciation in all 881.
The first issue there -- alleged massive frauds and illegal electoral practices -- failed for want of any evidence from either side, leaving the case to turn on revision and appreciation alone.

The rules of appreciation recited: the cardinal objective of discovering and giving effect to the voter's intention, the presumption of validity, invalidity of ballots prepared by one person or filled by two distinct persons, the marked-ballot rules on repeated names, and the Neighborhood, Intent and Idem Sonans Rules for claimed ballots.
The outcome in Bataan: final totals of 75,833 for Garcia and 74,416 for Roman, widening the margin to 1,417, and the unanimous dismissal on September 22, 2005 of both protest and counter-protest.

Angping v. Roces: Zenaida Angping's substitution for her husband Harry, whose Certificate of Candidacy the Comelec First Division cancelled by a resolution 'deemed promulgated' on April 30, 2004, and Comelec Resolution No. 6823 denying due course to her substitute candidacy.

The Tribunal's ruling through Rep. Mauricio G. Domogan: Miranda v. Abaya did not apply because the withdrawal and substitution preceded the actual issuance of the cancelling resolution, the substitution was allowed under Section 77 of the Omnibus Election Code, and Resolution No. 6823 was a mere administrative issuance void for want of the notice and hearing required for quasi-judicial action under Section 78.

The vote of 6-2-1 holding the protestant a proper party, the affirmative finding of jurisdiction, the rejection of the forum-shopping charge, and the observation that the protestee had been proclaimed on a mere 6,347 votes amid the district's high voting population.

CJP's Separate Opinion in Angping: the allegations sufficed to confer jurisdiction, the protestee's 'prejudicial questions' were no ground for immediate dismissal, review of Resolution No. 6823 was not dispositive, and the primordial duty of the Tribunal was to ascertain the true winner in the election.

His jurisdictional checklist -- a protestant who duly filed a Certificate of Candidacy and was voted for, a proclaimed protestee, and filing within ten days -- and the basic rule that jurisdiction is determined by the allegations of the petition, regardless of entitlement to the relief sought.

His reasons for finding no forum shopping: the certiorari petition in the Supreme Court sought only nullification of Resolution No. 6823 and could not have declared a winner, while the protest sought a re-canvassing to find the true and lawful winner.

The subsequent proceedings: simultaneous revision and re-canvassing ordered, the protestee's withdrawal of revision in the unrevised precincts granted on June 22, 2005, suspension under the Supreme Court's TRO of June 28, 2005, and the Court's Decision of September 15, 2005 sustaining the HRET by a vote of 8-4-3 and lifting the TRO.

The pending cases: seven protests already revised, with 100 percent revision ordered in Candazo v. De Guzman, Roman v. Garcia, Gatchalian v. Carlos, Tiquia v. Serapio and Jaafar v. Abubakar, and the rest at the evidence and appreciation stages.

The conclusion: his confidence that, barring unforeseen events like a Supreme Court TRO, the HRET would decide all its cases within the first two years of its three-year term, followed by a commendation of the members and a full roll of the Secretariat's officers.

stances.claim: The primordial duty of the Tribunal is to ascertain the true winner in the election, so questions about the truthfulness or merit of a protestant's claims belong to the regular course of the proceedings, not to a motion to dismiss.
stances.rhetorical_move: purpose-over-technicality argument, anchored in the basic rule that jurisdiction is determined by the allegations of the petition regardless of entitlement to the relief asserted

stances.claim: Zenaida Angping's petition sufficiently alleged every essential jurisdictional fact -- a duly filed Certificate of Candidacy and votes received, a proclaimed protestee, and filing within the ten-day reglementary period -- so the HRET properly assumed jurisdiction.
stances.rhetorical_move: checklist verification, matching each jurisdictional requisite against the unrefuted dates and averments on record

stances.claim: There was no forum shopping, because the certiorari petition in the Supreme Court sought only the nullification of Comelec Resolution No. 6823 and could not have declared who won, while the election protest sought a re-canvassing to find the true and lawful winner.
stances.rhetorical_move: relief-by-relief comparison of the two actions to show the objectives were not identical

stances.claim: The HRET has been diligent in its work and its members have shown admirable doggedness, prudence and speed, so that barring unforeseen events like a Supreme Court TRO it should decide all its cases within the first two years of its three-year term.
stances.rhetorical_move: performance report backed by counts -- more than half the docket disposed of within the first year -- ending in a forecast qualified by an explicit caveat

stances.claim: Residence in election law is synonymous with domicile, and an individual does not lose domicile merely by living and maintaining residences in different places; a change requires an actual and deliberate abandonment of the previous one.
stances.rhetorical_move: reported as the Tribunal's holding in San Miguel v. Dy, applying Romualdez-Marcos v. Comelec and placing the burden on the petitioner

notable_anecdotes: CJP writes the chapter to redeem a promise made in 'Leveling the Playing Field,' where he had said he enjoyed his role as HRET chairperson and saluted his brethren-lawmakers for their legal wisdom and judicial detachment.

He marks his first anniversary as HRET chairperson on July 15, 2005, a post he held concurrently with his seat on the Supreme Court, and notes that all the Tribunal's cases were new and at their nascent stage when he took over.

He recounts the cockpit-arena allegation in San Miguel v. Dy, where the petitioner claimed the address on Rep. Dy's Certificate of Candidacy was a cockpit stadium and she answered that its second floor had rooms and amenities serving as a residential area where she received visitors and conducted official business.

He relates the Bataan recount's irony: Roman protested 479 precincts alleging massive fraud, neither side presented any evidence of fraud, and after revision and appreciation of all 881 precincts Garcia's winning margin grew from 803 votes to 1,417.

He notes that the protestee in Angping v. Roces had been proclaimed on a mere 6,347 votes amid the high voting population of the Third District of Manila, and that the Tribunal's proceedings were halted by a Supreme Court TRO before the Court itself sustained the HRET by a vote of 8-4-3.

He closes with a personal surprise: on August 25, 2005 Atty. Noel Mapili, an HRET Attorney VI, privately presented him with a poem entitled 'AVP' encased in a petite wooden frame, which CJP reproduces verbatim in appreciation.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 22 of 'Judicial Renaissance' is Panganiban's report on the House of Representatives Electoral Tribunal, written to redeem a promise made in 'Leveling the Playing Field' and timed to his first anniversary as chairperson on July 15, 2005. He sets out the HRET's constitutional charter under Section 17, Article VI -- sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns and qualifications of representatives -- names its nine members as of October 10, 2005, and explains its practice: an election protest by a defeated candidate, a quo warranto petition by any voter, the five grounds for summary dismissal under Rule 21, summons and answer, the preliminary conference, and then either reception of evidence before a hearing commissioner or the collection of ballot boxes followed by revision and appreciation of ballots. Of the 15 protests, 3 quo warranto petitions and 1 petition to re-canvass returns filed after the May 10, 2004 elections, 8 protests and all 3 quo warranto cases had been disposed of, and he lists each dismissal with its resolution number and dates. He gives fuller accounts of San Miguel v. Dy, where evidence of domicile of origin and animus revertendi defeated a residence challenge under Romualdez-Marcos v. Comelec; of Samson v. Crisologo, where an absolute pardon restoring full civil and political rights was held to remove every disability, and where jurisdiction was said to pass from the Comelec to the HRET upon proclamation; and of Roman v. Garcia, where neither side proved the alleged massive fraud and revision of all 881 precincts widened Garcia's margin from 803 to 1,417 votes under the Neighborhood, Intent and Idem Sonans Rules and the principle that ballot appreciation exists to give effect to the voter's intention. The chapter's centerpiece is Angping v. Roces, a novel petition for re-canvassing alone, in which the Tribunal upheld the substitute candidacy and its own jurisdiction and Panganiban wrote separately that the Tribunal's primordial duty was to ascertain the true winner. He closes by praising the Tribunal's diligence, forecasting that it would finish its cases within two years, commending the Secretariat by name, and reproducing a poem an HRET lawyer had privately given him.
